blocks.title: Grammar Lens — a number cannot stand alone

segments.text: In Japanese a number does not simply sit in front of a thing. It takes a counter — a small word behind the number that says what kind of thing is being counted. Wikipedia's article calls counters measure words used with numbers to count things, actions, and events, and English has a few of the same shape: two sheets of paper, three head of cattle.
You have been using one since chapter nine and nobody said so.
いちど — ichido — one time.
Its own lesson said: ichi is one, and do counts an occurrence. That ど is a counter. It counts occurrences, which is why いちど is one time and not one.
And the つ you spent all of last chapter on is a counter too — the general one. That is why nine of the ten native words carry it and とお does not.

blocks.title: You'll Want to Know — when to reach for it

segments.text: Japanese has a great many counters and you will not learn them all here. What you can learn in one sentence is the rule that gets you through:
When you do not know the counter, use the つ series. Up to ten it will carry almost any ordinary object.

That is exactly what Wikipedia says of the traditional numerals — that the problem of choosing can often be sidestepped by using them. ひとつ to とお, and no further, because that is where the series stops.
コーヒー ふたつ — two coffees. Nobody will blink.
The rule has an edge, and it is the next lesson: people and animals do not take つ. They have counters of their own and there is no way round it.
Say コーヒー ふたつ. Then say いちど and name the counter inside it.
What do you use when you do not know the counter? (つ, up to ten.)
Sources: Wikipedia: Japanese counter word; Wiktionary: hitotsu.

blocks.title: You'll Want to Know — hear and say

segments.text: にん — -nin — the counter for people.
Both signs are old. What is new is that it attaches to the borrowed numbers, not the native ones:

utterances: how many: three people. how you say it: さんにん.
how many: four people. how you say it: よにん.
how many: five people. how you say it: ごにん.
how many: ten people. how you say it: じゅうにん.

segments.text: さん plus にん (-nin), ご plus にん (-nin). Nothing changes. Four is the one to watch: it is よ, not よん — the native word again, and shorter here.
You have nine family words and until now no way to say how many of anything you had. こども さんにん — three children.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens — where the tsu rule stops

segments.text: Last lesson's rule had an edge, and this is it. つ never counts people. There is no hitotsu of a person; you cannot sidestep にん (-nin), and the same is true of animals, which have counters of their own.
So the rule now reads with both ends showing: use つ for ordinary things up to ten; use the proper counter for anything alive.
And にん (-nin) itself has an exception, at exactly two numbers. That is the next lesson.
Write にん (-nin). Say sannin, yonin, gonin, juunin. Then say こども さんにん.
Which number is odd in this list? (Four — よにん, not yonnin.)
Sources: Wikipedia: Japanese counter word.

segments.prompt: Can you count people with the tsu series? Say why or why not, and give three people in Japanese.

feedback.correct: That is the edge of the tsu rule.
feedback.incorrect: The tsu series covers ordinary objects, not anything alive.

segments.text: ひとり — hitori — one person.

Not ichinin. Not ninin. Every other number takes にん (-nin) and these two do not.
Every sign is yours: ひ and ふ came two chapters ago, と, た and り long before.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens — the seam, one more time

segments.text: Read the four words together and the exception stops looking like one:

utterances: number: one. native count: ひとつ. with the people counter: ひとり.
number: two. native count: ふたつ. with the people counter: ふたり.
number: three. native count: みっつ. with the people counter: さんにん.

segments.text: hito- and futa- are the same pieces you learned two chapters ago. At one and two, the native number walks into the borrowed counter and stays; from three on, the borrowed number takes over.

That is the third time you have seen this. At よん and なな the native word stood inside the borrowed count. Here the native word stands inside a borrowed counter. It is one seam, and it runs the whole length of Japanese numbers.
あね ひとり、あに ふたり — one elder sister, two elder brothers.
Write ひとり and ふたり. Say hitori, futari, sannin, yonin — and hear the switch happen between the second and the third.
Where does the switch happen? (Between two and three.)
Sources: Wikipedia: Japanese counter word.

blocks.title: Guided Practice — count what you have

segments.text: Chapter twelve gave you a face. Until this chapter you could name every part of it and say how many of nothing.
め ふたつ — two eyes みみ ふたつ — two ears はな ひとつ — one nose くち ひとつ — one mouth.
Four nouns, none of them alive on its own, so the つ rule covers all four without your having to know a thing about which counter a nose takes.

segments.text: ほ — ho.
Write は first. You have had it since chapter one: a left vertical, one horizontal, then the right stroke that loops at the foot.
ほ is that figure with one more horizontal, and Sirgazil's animation puts it above the one は already has. Four strokes, in this order:
the left vertical, hooking at the foot.
the upper horizontal on the right.
the lower horizontal on the right.
the right vertical, down through both bars and looping at the foot.
So the only thing you are learning is a bar, and where it goes.
ほ also finishes a set. Japanese's h-row runs ha, hi, fu, he, ho, and you now hold four of its five: は from chapter one, ひ and ふ from two chapters ago, and ほ here. Only へ is missing.
Write ひ once beside them and hear the row.
Write は, then ほ (ho) beneath it, and mark the stroke that differs.
Copy ほ (ho); hide it; write it again.
Say both aloud: ha, ho. Then say ひとつ and hear the same ひ.
How many strokes? (Four.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart; stroke count and order per KanjiVG and Sirgazil's Commons animation.

segments.prompt: Write ho, and say what makes it different from ha.
acceptedResponses: ほ — one extra horizontal, drawn above ha's

feedback.incorrect: Compare it with は: the difference is a single horizontal.

blocks.title: You'll Want to Know — hear and say

segments.text: ほん — -hon — the counter for long, thin things.

Wikipedia's list for it is worth reading whole: rivers, roads, train tracks, ties, pencils, bottles, guitars. Nothing on that list is a book, though the sign it is written with is 本 — the very kanji you have been writing since chapter five, inside 日本語.
That is the shape rule in one word: ほん (-hon) does not care what the thing is, only that it is longer than it is wide.
Two of your own words qualify. One of them you can already say:
あし にほん — two legs.
The other is かみ, a hair — and the word for one hair has to wait two lessons, because at one the counter changes shape.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens — the counter bends the sound

segments.text: にん (-nin) attached to the numbers and nothing moved. ほん (-hon) does not behave. Here are the four that leave it alone:

utterances: number: two. the form: にほん.
number: four. the form: よんほん.
number: five. the form: ごほん.
number: seven. the form: ななほん.

segments.text: At three the ほ takes the dakuten you have had since chapter three, and at one, six, eight and ten it goes further still — further than the dakuten can take it. Both of those need a mark on the sign, and the second mark is one this book has never taught. The next two lessons buy it and then spend it; until then, say the four plain ones.
Write ほん (-hon). Say nihon, yonhon, gohon, nanahon — the four that leave the counter alone. Then say あし にほん.
What does ほん (-hon) count? (Anything longer than it is wide.)
Sources: Wikipedia: Japanese counter word.

segments.prompt: Say two long thin things and four long thin things in Japanese.

feedback.correct: Both plain — the counter only bends at one, three, six, eight and ten.
feedback.incorrect: Two and four leave the counter alone.

segments.text: ゜ — the handakuten.
A small circle, written at the top right of a kana, in the same place the dakuten goes.
Japanese has exactly two of these marks and you have had one of them since chapter three:

utterances: mark: ゛ dakuten. what it does: voices the consonant. example: ほ (ho) becomes ぼ.
mark: ゜ handakuten. what it does: turns the h-row into p. example: ほ (ho) becomes ぽ.

segments.text: The handakuten works on one row only — the row は and ほ (ho) belong to. Nowhere else in the syllabary does it appear, which makes it the rarest thing in the writing system and the easiest to place: if you see the little circle, the sign under it is an h-row kana and the sound is p.
That row is the one you have just been filling in. ふ takes both marks too, giving bu and pu, and so does は. The mark is rare; the row is not.
Write the circle small. It is a circle, not a dot, and it does not touch the sign it sits on.
Write ほ (ho), then ぼ, then ぽ, and say all three.
Say the same three sounds on は, without writing them.
Check one thing: is the circle open?
Which row does the handakuten work on? (Only the h-row.)
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart, U+309C.

segments.prompt: Write ho, then the same sign with each of the two marks, and say all three.
acceptedResponses: ほ ぼ ぽ — ho, bo, po

feedback.correct: Two marks, one row, three sounds.
feedback.incorrect: The dakuten voices; the handakuten makes p.

blocks.title: You'll Want to Know — hear and say

segments.text: いっぽん — ippon — one long thin thing.
Not ichihon. The いち shortens to いっ, and the ほ takes the handakuten you learned last lesson.
Here is the whole counter, with the numbers this book can spell:

utterances: number: one. the form: いっぽん (ippon). what happens: p, and a held beat.
number: two. the form: にほん. what happens: plain.
number: three. the form: さんぼん. what happens: b.
number: four. the form: よんほん. what happens: plain.
number: five. the form: ごほん. what happens: plain.
number: six. the form: ろっぽん. what happens: p, and a held beat.
number: seven. the form: ななほん. what happens: plain.
number: eight. the form: はっぽん. what happens: p, and a held beat.
number: ten. the form: じゅっぽん. what happens: p, and a held beat.

segments.text: Nine is missing from that table on purpose. Its everyday form needs a sign this book has not taught, so it is left out rather than guessed at.

Read the shape of the rest: one, six, eight and ten all end in a held beat and take p. Three ends in the nasal ん and takes b. Everything else is plain. The counter is not being irregular — it is being pushed by the sound in front of it.
かみ いっぽん (ippon) — one hair.
Write いっぽん. Say the run: ippon, nihon, sanbon, yonhon, gohon, roppon. Then say かみ いっぽん.
Why is nine missing from the table? (Its form needs a sign this book has not taught.)
Sources: Wikipedia: Japanese counter word.

segments.prompt: Which numbers push the counter to p, and what do they all have in common?
acceptedResponses: one, six, eight and ten — they all end in a held beat

feedback.correct: The held beat is doing the work, not the number.
feedback.incorrect: Listen to the end of each number, not to its value.

segments.text: A number in Japanese does not stand on its own. It takes a counter, and the counter is chosen by what kind of thing is being counted:

utterances: the thing: an ordinary object, up to ten. the counter: つ.
the thing: a person. the counter: にん (-nin).
the thing: anything longer than it is wide. the counter: ほん (-hon).
the thing: an occurrence. the counter: ど, which you had in chapter nine.

segments.text: Both edges of that are worth carrying. Reach for つ when you do not know — up to ten it will carry almost any ordinary object. Do not reach for it for anything alive, and do not expect it past ten.

And the seam this book has been drawing since chapter fourteen runs through all of it. よん and なな: the native word inside the borrowed count. ひとり and ふたり: the native word inside a borrowed counter. Two counts, and the places where they touch are not random — they are the same handful of numbers, every time.
What do you use when you do not know the counter? (つ, to ten.) Where does that rule fail? (Anything alive.) Say one person and one hair. (ひとり; かみ いっぽん (ippon).)
